problem_markdown: Let $n\ge2$. Suppose $k^2+k+n$ is prime for every integer $0\le k\le\sqrt{n/3}$. Prove it is prime for every integer $0\le k\le n-2$.
solutions_markdown:
Write $F(k)=n+k(k+1)$ and $r=\lfloor\sqrt{n/3}\rfloor$. Induct from the assumed range. Suppose $r<b\le n-2$ and all earlier $F(i)$ are prime. Since $n<3b^2$, we have $F(b)<(2b+1)^2$.

For $b+1\le j\le2b$, put $i=j-b-1$, so $0\le i<b$. Then $F(b)-F(i)=(b-i)j$. If $F(b)$ and $j$ shared a prime divisor, it would divide the prime $F(i)$, so $F(i)\mid j$. But $j\le2b\le2n-4<2F(i)$, forcing $j=F(i)$. The equality $b+i+1=n+i(i+1)$ becomes $b+1=n+i^2$, impossible because $b\le n-2$. Thus $F(b)$ is coprime to every integer in $(b,2b]$.

Every integer $d\le b$ has a power-of-two multiple in $(b,2b]$, so $F(b)$ is also coprime to every $d\le b$. It has no divisor between 2 and $2b$, while its square root is below $2b+1$. Hence it is prime. This completes the induction; $n=2$ is already in the assumed range.
